questions.explanation: A policy is a statement of intent and a control is a mechanism, and the gap between them is where this example sits. Acknowledgement records that a person was told; it does not observe what they then do, and a rule with no observation and no consequence is a request, and requests are followed roughly in proportion to how inconvenient the alternative feels. What makes the policy real is a mechanism that produces a fact: a check on the workstation setting, a report of who has it disabled, and a defined consequence when the report shows someone has. The second option is the misunderstanding that gets a signed acknowledgement treated as compliance evidence, and it is a genuine artefact for showing that people were informed, which is a different and much weaker claim. The third and fourth are both reasonable-sounding refinements that address a real secondary problem, and neither changes the fact that nothing here observes behaviour. This is the same shape as the difference between a requirement and an implementation, and it recurs wherever a document is offered as a control.
questions.hint: Ask what happens the next morning, and who finds out.

questions.explanation: The important property of this kind of document is that it is written in terms of what must be demonstrable rather than what must be bought, and that is a deliberate design choice rather than vagueness. It means two organisations meeting the same requirement can have entirely different estates, and a reader assessing either of them has to ask how the outcome was achieved rather than what was installed. It also means adoption is a decision with a cost attached, since satisfying a control the estate does not already have is a project, and the mapping between the standard's wording and the estate's actual mechanisms is the work that decides whether the claim is true. The second option is the belief behind a great deal of anxious compliance behaviour, and it is not how a published voluntary standard works; where something is genuinely binding it is binding because a law, a contract or a licence says so, and that is a different instrument. The third is a serious misreading, and it produces the common pattern of a framework adopted wholesale and then abandoned, because the prescribed parts are the parts nobody wanted. The fourth is the opposite of the design, since naming products is what the document avoids.
questions.hint: Ask whether it says what to buy or what to be able to show.

questions.explanation: Separating the objective from the mechanism is the single most useful habit in control work, because it is what lets an estate improve without renegotiating the requirement, and it is what lets two very different estates both be assessed against the same requirement. Here the objective is a decision about access made by a person at least four times a year with a name against it and an outcome recorded, and the monthly report plus confirmation is a reasonable way to produce that: the frequency is higher and the judgement is still human. What would not satisfy it is a report that is generated, filed and never confirmed, because the objective names a reviewer and a decision, and neither is present in a bare export. The second option is the misconception that makes frameworks rigid and is why a well-written one is written in outcome terms. The third is the failure mode of metric-chasing, where a number is optimised and the judgement it was meant to prompt disappears. The fourth is the half that is easy to check and the half that is not: a signature line can be written by anyone.

questions.explanation: A compensating control is an argument that the risk is handled by another route, and the argument has to survive two questions. The first is whether it addresses the same risk, and this is where most alternatives fail: a control that addresses a neighbouring risk is not a substitute, and the test is to describe the scenario the requirement was written for and then show how the alternative changes what happens in that scenario. The second is whether the control is real, which means tested, owned and time-limited, and a mechanism that is believed to work but has never been exercised is a hope. The review date is the part that gets left out, and its absence is what turns a compensating control into a quiet permanent exception: the original problem was never solved, the discussion closed, and the next person to look finds a documented control and no reason to look further. The second and third options both reduce this to paperwork, and transparency is genuinely valuable but it is not a mechanism that stops anything happening. The fourth is close to right and slightly wrong, since most compensating controls do become permanent, and the honest response is to set the date at which either the requirement or the alternative is dealt with.
questions.hint: Ask what happens in the scenario the original control was written for, and ask when this will be looked at again.

questions.explanation: An entry with a description, two scores and a name is a well-formed list of worries, and a review meeting that reads it can rank the worries and nothing more. What makes an entry a commitment is that it names what will be done, by when, and what the exposure looks like afterwards, and the third of those is the one that is most often missing and most worth having: a treatment with no stated residual position is a treatment whose effect nobody will ever check, and the next version of the register will simply carry the original score forward unchanged, which is indistinguishable from having done nothing. The name is necessary and not sufficient, since accountability without a task is a distribution list. The second option is the belief that a score communicates a decision, and a score communicates a comparison. The third is a defensible opinion about well-written descriptions and it does not produce a date, and a date is what a review sorts on. The fourth is a real weakness of name-only entries, since without a task the owner has nothing to report.

questions.explanation: The role exists because most risks are owned by people who cannot act on them, and putting a name against an entry that nobody can influence produces a register that looks governed and is not. The useful accountability is procedural and it is real: the owner is the person who has to make sure the risk appears in front of someone with the authority and the budget to decide about it, that a decision is reached rather than deferred indefinitely, and that the decision and its date are written down where the next reader can find them. That is work, it can be done badly, and it can be checked. The second option converts a governance role into an indemnity, which no organisation can actually agree to and which would make the role impossible to fill. The third is not what a name is for, and if the name is a non-specialist the value is in the chasing rather than the expertise. The fourth describes a role that has no present-tense accountability, and it is the most common way these entries quietly stop moving.

questions.explanation: The difference between the two is a decision and everything that makes a decision, and the first thing a decision needs is a decider: someone with the authority and the budget to accept the exposure, who is not the person who wants to ship. Given that, three things make it real rather than cosmetic. The acceptance is written down in terms of what remains, so the next reader is not left to guess. It states the conditions under which it stops being acceptable, which is the part that converts an open-ended decision into a manageable one, since a triggering condition is what lets it be revisited without a debate about whether it should be. And it has a date, so it cannot quietly persist for years while everyone assumes somebody approved it. The second option is the reasoning that produces most of these entries, and its failure is that the residual score is the least reliable field in the register, computed by whoever last touched it. The third is a signature on a form, which records that a signature happened rather than that a judgement was made, and the signature is frequently obtained by routing it to the person least likely to read it. The fourth puts a date on a deferral without adding a decider, and a dated deferral is still a deferral.

questions.explanation: The categories describe what happens to the exposure, and the supplier case is transfer because the consequence of the supplier's failure falls on the supplier, subject to what the contract provides. What makes a transfer real rather than nominal is the enforceability behind it, and that is the part to examine: an assessment report is a description of the supplier's controls and carries no remedy, while a contract with a stated security obligation, a right to be told about a problem, and a right to terminate gives the organisation something it can actually use. Without those, a transfer is a claim on paper that becomes a claim in a dispute after the data has gone. The second option is the category people reach for by habit, and controls of the organisation's own do not reduce a supplier's handling of the data; they can reduce what leaves the organisation or how it is checked, which is genuinely useful and is mitigation of a different risk. The third is available and is a legitimate business decision rather than a technical one, and the fact that it has not been chosen means the activity continues. The fourth is what a completed assessment is often recorded as, and the assessment describes rather than accepts, and the acceptance decision has to be made by someone.

questions.explanation: Completion is a fact about the administration of a module: who was assigned it and who opened it. Behaviour under pressure is a different fact, measured differently, and the gap between them is where the interesting failures sit. This matters because the number is close to universal in reporting and is read as a result rather than as an input, so a programme that has become very good at distributing modules can be getting steadily worse at the thing it exists for, and the trend line will show improvement throughout. What would show a change in behaviour is a measure taken from a situation where the decision is real: whether people report suspicious messages rather than opening them, how quickly a reported message is recognised as one somebody else also saw, whether a person asks before granting an unusual permission. The second option is the inference everyone draws and it is not supported by anything in the figure. The third is a genuine gap worth looking at, since six per cent of an estate is a few hundred people, but it is a statement about assignment rather than about awareness. The fourth is true of badly written modules and false as a general claim, and it is the belief that gets a well-designed programme replaced with a checkbox.

questions.explanation: The aggregate is the problem. A single percentage over everybody mixes the people who were reached by training with the people who were not, and as the trained group grows the aggregate rises for a reason that has nothing to do with the untrained group's behaviour, so the number improves while the number that would matter is flat. Any figure like this has to be broken at least by whether the recipient has had the training and how recently, and reported against a denominator that is the messages actually delivered rather than the messages sent, since undelivered messages count as not reported in most implementations. The other dimension worth adding is what happened after the report, since a report that arrives too late to stop the credential being entered has not prevented anything. The second option is a category error: the filter and the awareness programme are different controls, and a reported message is a signal about the recipient rather than about the filter. The third has the direction backwards, since a low report rate is the problem and there is no general target number worth quoting. The fourth is a real design consideration, and it argues for varying the messages, but it is not a defect in the reporting.

questions.explanation: An exception is a temporary decision, and the thing that makes it temporary is the date. Without one, the original problem is never revisited: the arrangement that justified it changes, the people who approved it move on, and the next person to encounter the gap reads a file that says the policy does not apply here for a reason that no longer describes the situation, and has no way to tell that from a live decision. The common end state is worse than the original gap, because the policy looks enforced everywhere except in one documented place, and the documentation is what a reviewer relies on. A date does not have to mean the gap gets fixed; it means somebody is required to look, and the outcome of that look can be a fresh acceptance with a new date. The second option inverts the logic of a review process, since low-level approvals are what a review exists to catch rather than what invalidates them. The third and fourth name fields that are genuinely required, and this record has them, which is why the question is about the fifth field rather than about the first four.

The things that move it are what the system holds, who can reach it, what else depends on it, and what would have to be true for an attacker to use the gap, and each of those has to come from the auditor's understanding of the estate rather than from the control's name. questions.explanation: A deadline works by concentrating effort on a bounded set, and a blanket extension dissolves that set. The items in it do not each get a shorter window with a hard end; they get a common end that is far enough away that none of them is urgent today, and a finding that is not urgent on any particular day does not get worked on, which is not a prediction but the standard observed behaviour. The second option is true and is exactly the problem, because the items in the set were the ones carrying the risk and the items left behind are by definition not carrying it. The third is a real capacity problem with a real answer, and the answer is a decision about which items get the capacity, made explicitly, with the residual risk accepted by name rather than by silence. Asking for a single extension across a set is the shape to avoid because it cannot distinguish the one item that genuinely cannot wait from the nine that simply have not been started, and by the next review the extension is the new normal. The fourth inverts the accountability, since a deadline set without reference to capacity is the thing to correct, but that is done by resetting it deliberately rather than by letting it drift.

questions.explanation: The purpose of a tier is to answer the question a flat deadline cannot, which is what to do first when there is not enough capacity to do everything. Severity encodes consequence and reachability, and sorting by it means the item with the worst combination is at the top of the list rather than whichever was published first, and that is a genuine efficiency as well as a fairness argument. questions.explanation: Publication is the point at which the description of the flaw becomes available to anyone, including parties who were not looking, and the estate's state does not change at that moment at all. Everything between publication and deployment is a window in which the described weakness is present on systems that have it, and the schedule is a statement about how wide that window is permitted to be rather than a mitigation of it. What genuinely narrows the window are actions on the estate's side: removing the affected component or the feature, cutting reach so the component is not exposed to untrusted input, or putting a control in front of the specific behaviour the weakness needs. Each of those can be done faster than a rebuild and often much faster, and the discipline is to establish which of the three applies before assuming a patch is the only route. The second option has the causality exactly backwards, since a fix existing is what makes the window closable rather than what makes the flaw live. The third is the reading that makes the window invisible, because it treats the publication date as the start of the problem rather than as the start of the knowledge. The fourth is a genuine limitation on one route and not on the others, and the supplier's own schedule is outside the organisation's control while its own configuration is not.
questions.hint: Ask what the estate looks like on the Wednesday, and what could change that before the fix lands.

questions.explanation: Every question that matters starts from the inventory, and the inventory is the one artefact that cannot be derived from a single authoritative source because it spans procurement, deployment, retirement and naming, each of which is recorded somewhere else and none of which is the inventory. The drift is therefore not a data quality problem that shows up in a report; it means the organisation cannot answer whether a given system is one it is responsible for, which is the first question asked during an investigation, an assessment and a scoping exercise. Systems nobody listed are not scanned, not patched and not included in any decision, and a system listed after it has been retired generates work that finds nothing. The second option is the visible symptom and it is the least important one. The third confuses a periodic correction with a current state, and an annual reconciliation is a point in time rather than a mechanism, so the drift returns within weeks. questions.explanation: The check is a comparison between two states and its output is a difference, which is exactly its value and exactly its limit. It is very good at finding the change nobody made: a hand-edited setting during an incident, a resource created directly in the console, a provider feature that altered something as a side effect, an automated tool with more reach than the team realised. It is completely silent on the question of whether the baseline is a good baseline, because that question is a judgement made once by people and then encoded, and a wrong baseline faithfully enforced is a stable wrong configuration. That is why baseline changes go through review and why a check that starts reporting large volumes of differences is often a sign the baseline was updated rather than that the estate degraded. The second option is the over-reading that makes drift checking feel like a security control in itself. The third under-reads it, since a checked baseline is how a good configuration is kept. The fourth confuses a mechanism with an outcome, since the check reports a difference whether or not anybody acts on it.

questions.explanation: The control is a bet on attention, and the bet is that a second person looking at the same change will notice something the first is not motivated to notice, whether that is an unnecessary permission, a destructive step or an unfamiliar destination. That is a reasonable bet for a change nobody is trying to rush and a poor one under pressure, which is why the interesting question is not whether two names are on the approval but whether the roles are genuinely held by different people in practice. A process slow enough that people work around it produces a record with two names and one author, and the artefact then provides assurance about nothing while looking like it provides assurance about something. The second option is the assumption that makes emergency changes the standard case, and the mechanism for handling those is a separate path that is logged afterwards, which reintroduces the single-person step openly rather than hiding it in the ordinary one. The third confuses rank with independence, since a junior person noticing something is worth more than a senior one waving it through, and the two do not have to be ordered. The fourth misunderstands the control entirely: it is about behaviour and about the incentive to approve one's own work.

questions.explanation: A cadence is a statement about the rate of change and the rate of consequence, and both differ sharply within a single set. Standing administrator rights are the most valuable thing a person can hold and are granted in small numbers, which is exactly the argument for reviewing them often, since a small set is cheap to review and the consequence of a stale one is high. Break-glass credentials are a different problem: they are designed to be unused, so a review that shows nobody used them is a good result rather than a waste, and the things worth checking about them are whether they still work, whether they are still stored correctly and whether their use is recorded. Database ownership changes when people change jobs and is the one most likely to be quietly held by someone who has left the team that used it. The second option is administratively attractive and it forces the highest-consequence items into the same interval as the least, which is the same error as a single remediation deadline. The third is a work estimate rather than a risk judgement. The fourth builds the cadence around the evidence requirement, which is a category error: the review exists to find stale access, and sizing it to a sample guarantees that anything outside the sample is never reviewed at all.

questions.explanation: The recertification is a well-posed question asked of a person who can answer it: does this person still need this access. It is genuinely effective at that, and it removes the large population of rights that were needed for a role somebody has since moved out of, which is the most common way access accumulates. What it structurally cannot find is access nobody asked about, because the list is the question. Rights granted outside the process, rights inherited through group membership that nobody thought of as a grant, a service account created under a different name and never added to anyone's list, an entitlement that arrived through a migration: all of these are absent from the list, and a manager confirming a list is a good check of the list rather than a check of the estate. That is the honest framing and it determines what to add rather than whether to keep the process. What makes it stronger is comparing the review against something independent: the set of people who have actually used each entitlement over a period, since a right nobody has used in months is a question the list cannot pose, and reconciling the list against the joiner, mover and leaver record catches the case where the list is right and the person has left. The process is not a substitute for generating the list well, and the failures people remember are the ones where it was treated as if it were.

questions.explanation: The volume of data leaving an organisation in a leaver's departure is far larger than the list of systems they were formally entitled to, and that is the point. Copies accumulate: exports in a personal folder, a working copy on a laptop, a synchronised file, a spreadsheet assembled for a meeting, a set of photographs of a whiteboard. Revoking the account on the last day closes the systems and does nothing about the copies, and the copies leave quietly during the weeks between the decision and the departure, which is when the organisation is still relying on good behaviour from somebody it has already decided to lose. The useful responses all attach to the same interval: collect the data during it, require the return of anything held locally, ask the person to attest to what they have copied, and transfer or archive the working material before the day rather than after. The second option is the false premise behind the first, and it is worth rejecting directly: a disabled account does not prevent a copy that has already been made, which is the entire reason people exfiltrate before they leave rather than after. The third names a real requirement and describes the wrong interval, since deletion at the point of departure addresses the account's contents rather than the copies. The fourth is a detail and the copy is already out by then.

questions.explanation: Retention is usually argued about as a cost question and it is really a data question, because what you keep is exactly what you have promised to be able to show, and it is available to whoever can read the store. Audit records in particular contain more than the events people expect: they name individuals, they record what was accessed and when, and over a long enough period they describe the working pattern of the whole organisation. That makes the archive worth protecting to a standard the live logs never needed, because it is the most complete internal description available, and it makes access to it worth logging as carefully as the activity it records. The consequences to decide are the real answer to this question: who may search the archive, whether a search is itself recorded, how an archive is protected against the party whose activity is in it, and what is deleted at the end of the period rather than retained indefinitely. The second option is the framing that gets a long retention adopted without those decisions being taken. The third is a misreading of the word retention, and a practice that quietly drops early is one an auditor or a court will notice. The fourth confuses keeping with reviewing, and the two are managed by different people on different cycles.
questions.hint: Ask who can read what will be in that archive, and what it will describe about them.

questions.explanation: Two distinct obligations are packed into the statement and they need two different mechanisms. The collection limit is a decision made at the point a field is added, and the only place it can be enforced is in the form and the interface, since a field nobody collects cannot be leaked, exported or subpoenaed later; that is a design and review question about what the form asks. The deletion duty is a lifecycle question, and the only version of it that works is one the system performs, because a schedule that depends on somebody remembering produces a collection of records that are all past their date and none of them gone. Anonymisation or irreversible aggregation is the other honest route where the data is still wanted in aggregate. The second option is the paperwork version and it is a real obligation of its own, and it is what almost every assessment looks at, which is why the technical version has to be named separately. The third protects what is collected and says nothing about whether it should have been collected, and encryption is compatible with holding far too much for far too long. The fourth is access control, which is a different obligation again and an important one, and it addresses neither of these.

questions.explanation: Both halves of the request are hard for the same reason, which is that the organisation is rarely sure where the data about one person is. The data lives in the primary systems, in exports sent elsewhere, in derived and aggregated copies that may no longer be separable from other people, in backups that are not queryable but that still contain the record, and in the systems of processors who hold it on the organisation's behalf. A response that produces the primary record and misses the rest is not a complete response, and in a deletion request an incomplete one leaves the organisation unable to state truthfully that the data is gone. The work is therefore a discovery exercise before it is a production one, and the useful preparation is a map of where personal data is held and who each holder is, maintained before any request arrives. The second option is the assumption that makes the first request easy and the second one wrong. The third is wrong in a way that matters: an open investigation does not suspend a privacy obligation, and a refusal made on those grounds is exactly the kind of decision that gets challenged. The fourth understates the first step, since establishing whose records are in scope is what prevents a response that discloses one person's data to another.

questions.explanation: The clock is written in terms of awareness rather than confirmation, and the reason is that an organisation that could have known but chose not to look must not benefit from the delay it created. That places the organisation in an uncomfortable position, because the trigger is a judgement about what it reasonably should have known at a moment when the facts are still incomplete, and the judgement is made by the same people who would prefer to investigate for another week. The practical consequence is that the period has to be reserved and the initial notification has to be capable of being made on partial information, with the detail supplied as it becomes available, rather than the notification being treated as the end of the investigation. What makes this manageable is deciding in advance who decides, on what basis, and what the first version of the message says, because an unassigned decision made under pressure is a decision made late. The second option is the reading that makes the obligation safe to ignore, and the gap between deciding and knowing is precisely what the obligation is designed to close. The third has the logic exactly backwards, since a party who found out first has simply removed the organisation's ignorance. The fourth is the practical difficulty the first answer creates, and it is answered by reserving capacity to say what is known and when more will follow.

questions.explanation: The uncomfortable property of this kind of request is the span. A report says the control is in place, and the control is a mechanism that operates continuously or not at all, so a question about two years is a question about two years of evidence rather than a single demonstration today, and the artefacts that answer it are the ones that were generated as a by-product of the control running: the reports it produced, the exceptions it raised, the reviews it recorded, the changes it caught. An organisation that designed for this keeps evidence as a matter of course. An organisation that did not discovers that its only artefact is a policy, which is a statement of intent and answers a different question, and the honest response at that point is to say what exists and what does not rather than to assemble something that reads well. The second option is the assumption behind most external attestations and it is a misunderstanding of scope: such a report covers a period and a system, and it says nothing about the specific control at the specific moment asked about. The third has the difficulty backwards, since a request about the past is harder to satisfy and is the one to prepare for. The fourth is the failure this question is aimed at, and it is worth noting that a policy plus no records is indistinguishable from a policy plus unrecorded activity.

questions.explanation: Checkable evidence has a shape and the shape is what makes it verifiable rather than persuasive. It is generated by the mechanism rather than written about it, so it exists whether or not anybody is reporting, which is the property a narrative cannot have. And it can be reproduced, so a reader can run the same query and get the same answer, which is the test that distinguishes a record from a claim. Applied to the three common cases: a control that produces a report can supply the report, a control that produces exceptions can supply the exception list, and a control that is a person making a judgement can supply a dated record of the decision with the name against it, and the third is the one most often offered as a description instead. The second option inverts the test, since the purpose of evidence is to constrain what the author can say rather than to make the reader comfortable. The third confuses length with rigour. The fourth is a real property of a document and not evidence of a control, since a signature attests to the signer's confidence rather than to the control's operation.

Recording it early and honestly is what protects the organisation later, and it is also the cheapest way to avoid the situation where two people remember the discovery differently. Containment comes second, with the caveat that it has to be done without destroying what the investigation needs, since the instinct to wipe and reinstall is the one that removes the evidence of what happened. Establishing the population affected comes third, and it is the step that determines the size of the notification and the shape of the message, and it is a real piece of work rather than a query, because the data is rarely in one place. Preparing the notification comes last but has to be ready before the clock matters, since the useful practice is a message that can be issued on partial facts and improved afterwards, rather than a final version that arrives too late. Independence is restored by moving the consequence away from the tester, and that can be done several ways. The test can be run by somebody who does not own the control and whose own assessment is not affected by its result. The evidence can be reconciled by a second person with no stake in it. The scope can be set by the recipient of the assurance rather than by the team being assured. A deliberately sampled check can be commissioned by someone outside the team, and the sample chosen by them. The second option is the intuitive defence of internal verification and it is true that the team knows more, which is exactly why the knowledge is not the constraint; the constraint is what the person is measured on. The third is a real phenomenon in some controls and has nothing to do with independence. The count can rise because there are more attacks, which is a security finding. It can rise because there is more legitimate traffic, which is a capacity finding. And it can rise because the estate grew, which is neither. Only the first is a change in risk, and the figure as presented cannot distinguish them, so the honest report carries the number of sign-ins presented alongside the number blocked, which turns three different stories into one number that separates them. The same applies to a great many security figures and the pattern is worth recognising: blocked attempts, alerts raised, vulnerabilities found, tickets closed, and every one of them moves with the volume of work passing through the system. The second option is the error that makes such a report comfortable, since more blocked sounds like more success and the underlying ratio may have fallen. answer.exemplar: The general answer is that a metric is a function of the estate, and the estate has more than one degree of freedom, so a rising value is consistent with several very different realities and only one of them is the one the reader is hoping for. There are four ways this happens and they are worth separating because each needs a different fix. The population can change: a quarter of devices is replaced and the replacements arrive configured, so the coverage figure rises substantially while every device that was already counted is exactly as it was, and nothing was configured this quarter. The unit of count can change, or the denominator can drift, so the same number now describes a different thing than it did last quarter and the comparison is meaningless. The work can move to somewhere it is not counted, so a control that used to happen in a monitored place now happens in an unmonitored one and the figure is accurate and useless. And the counted property may not be the protective one, which is the most important of the four: a setting can be enabled while the material it protects sits somewhere the setting does not reach, and a great many controls have exactly this shape, where the setting is necessary and the arrangement is what actually protects. The reason all four survive in practice is that a rising number is good news, so nobody interrogates it, and the cost of a metric that cannot fail is that it cannot be believed when it does. What a metric has to include before it can be used for a decision is therefore three things. The denominator, so the figure is a rate and the population it describes is explicit and does not change silently. A statement of what the counted property is sufficient for, which is the question that separates the fourth failure from the other three and which forces the reader to say what would have to be true for the setting to matter. And a second, independent measure produced by the mechanism rather than by the inventory, because a configuration count says what is enabled and a record of the mechanism running says what happened, and only the second can be trusted to fall when something breaks. The practical test is simple and worth applying to any figure in a dashboard: name three things that could have changed the number without anybody doing any work, and if three exist the number cannot carry a decision on its own.

It needs a denominator, a statement of what the property is sufficient for, and an independent measure produced by the mechanism rather than the inventory, since only the last can be expected to fall when something breaks.

answer.exemplar: The two disagree for a structural reason rather than a dishonest one, and the structural reason is that they are produced in completely different ways. An assessment is written by people who are describing a programme they know well, from a scale whose descriptions they recognise themselves in, at a point in time when the programme is a story about intentions and partly a story about work in progress. The evidence is produced by things that ran. A recertification that removed four hundred entitlements, a patching record with a median of nine days, a drift check that found a difference last Tuesday, a set of access requests sampled and refused: each of those exists because a mechanism operated and left a trace, and none of them is comfortable or chosen. When the two disagree, and they often do, the mechanism is usually right and the description is usually behind, because a programme that has genuinely improved still describes the programme it was last year, and because people filling in a scale tend to answer with the intent rather than the recent history. The evidence is also the more specific of the two, which matters when the two suggest different actions: a score of four out of five on recovery and a set of written procedures that have never been exercised are both true, and only one of them tells you what will happen. The corollary is that the two are not the same kind of artefact and averaging them is meaningless, so a report that presents a scale position next to a table of evidence is asking the reader to do the reconciliation, and a good one does that reconciliation explicitly rather than letting the two sit side by side. Which should govern a decision made on the strength of the assessment is the evidence, and the reason is worth stating carefully because it is not a claim that the people writing the assessment are unreliable. It is that the evidence is closer to the thing being decided about, since a decision about whether the programme can absorb a change depends on what the mechanisms have actually done rather than on how well the programme is described. The exception worth naming is a gap in the evidence, because absence of a record is not a record of absence and a control that genuinely does not generate anything cannot be assessed by its outputs. Where that is the case the answer is to start generating the record, and to treat the absence as the finding. The practical discipline is to make the assessment cite the artefact for every claim, which converts it from a description into a collection of references, and a claim that cannot be given a reference is then visibly a claim rather than a fact.

questions.explanation: An assessment is written from intent and self-knowledge while the evidence is produced by mechanisms that ran, so the description tends to lag the position and the evidence tends to be closer to what a decision depends on. The evidence governs, with the exception that a control generating no record cannot be assessed by its outputs and the absence is itself the finding; the fix is to make every assessment claim cite an artefact.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two was produced by running something and which by writing something.

answer.exemplar: The reason a request of this kind is a systems problem is that almost nobody in an organisation can say where the data about one person is, and the request cannot be answered until somebody can. The primary systems are the part everybody remembers, and they are the part where a query finds the record quickly. Everything else is the part that turns a request from an afternoon into a project. Exports sent to a processor, and what that processor then did with them. Derived and aggregated copies that may no longer be separable from other people, where a deletion request cannot be satisfied as asked and the honest answer is that the record has become anonymous. Backups, which are not queryable at all and which still contain the record, so the accurate statement is that the data has been superseded rather than erased, and that is a different sentence from the one the request asks for. Analytics and reporting copies built from a warehouse. Shared drives, mailboxes and note-taking archives that carry a person's name in a document nobody modelled. And third parties, who hold it on the organisation's behalf and who need to be told, which takes time the requester does not have. Two halves of the request are affected in opposite directions and the difference matters. A copy that is produced incompletely is misleading in the direction the requester cares about, and an erasure performed partially leaves the organisation unable to state truthfully that the data is gone, which is the harder of the two to recover from. What should be in place before the first request arrives is a map. A maintained inventory of the categories of personal data held, which system and which team holds each, who the processors are, and what the retention period is, so that the work of answering a request is a matter of following a list rather than of investigating. Alongside it, two or three other things: an identity check procedure, since a request can be satisfied in the wrong direction and the check has to be proportionate; a template of the response that can be issued on partial information with a stated date for the rest, because the honest answer is often a first response followed by a completion; and a decided position on backups, derived data and processors, taken in advance, since those are the three answers that cannot be produced under pressure. None of this is expensive and all of it is only worth having if it exists before the request, because the alternative is the discovery work happening while a clock is running.

questions.explanation: Almost nobody can say where one person's data is held, because it is spread across primary systems, exports, derived aggregates, non-queryable backups and processors, and the map does not exist until somebody builds it. The preparation is that map plus a proportionate identity check, a response template that can be issued on partial facts, and a decided position on backups, derived data and processors, all taken before the clock is running.

answer.exemplar: A completion figure is a fact about the administration of a course and the behaviour a security awareness programme exists to influence is a fact about a decision made under pressure by somebody who has been busy. Those are two different things and the number available to almost every organisation is the first one, because the first one is free and the second one requires either a simulation or an incident. It is worth being precise about the gap, because the gap is where the failures live. A module can be completed at ninety-four per cent while the remaining six per cent is a few hundred people who are never reached, and a few hundred people is a large enough population to run a campaign against. The aggregate itself moves with the size of the trained group, so a quarter in which the module is pushed hard produces a better figure whether or not the untrained group changed at all, which means the trend rewards the easy lever. And the number cannot distinguish a person who recognised the message and reported it from a person who did nothing, which is the same as a person who acted on it. The specific failure this hides is a report that arrives too late to matter: a message reported after the credential has been entered is a good outcome for the recipient and no outcome for the organisation, and a programme that counts only the arrival cannot see the difference. So what would have to be measured instead, stated in the order of usefulness, is this. Whether people report rather than act, measured against a denominator of messages actually delivered rather than sent, since undelivered messages count as not reported in most implementations and quietly flatter the result. Whether the report arrived before anything was entered, which is the outcome the programme exists to produce and which is measurable by comparing the report time against the interaction. And the result broken down by whether the recipient has had the training and how recently, which is the only way to see whether the training is doing anything, since an aggregate over everybody moves with the population rather than with the behaviour. Two more worth having: whether a message that a recipient reported was also reported by others, which indicates the message was recognisable rather than lucky, and whether people ask before granting an unusual permission, which is a different decision from the email one and often the one that matters more. None of this requires a large programme, and the version that is achievable is a small simulation with a break-out by training recency and a measure of what happened afterwards, which is a very different artefact from a completion percentage and a far better one to put in front of anybody.

questions.explanation: Completion is a fact about administering a course, not about a decision made under pressure, and the aggregate moves with the size of the trained population rather than with the untrained group's behaviour, so it rewards the easy lever. What to measure instead is reports against messages actually delivered, whether the report preceded any interaction with the message, and the result broken down by how recently the recipient was trained.
questions.hint: Ask whether the number was produced by running something or by administering something.

questions.explanation: Ninety gigabytes a day for four hundred days is 36,000 gigabytes, which is 36 terabytes, since a terabyte is a million gigabytes. The second route gives the same answer by treating a terabyte as a thousand gigabytes and noting that four hundred days is a little over a year rather than exactly one, so 90 times 400 over 1000 is 36 with the extra fortnight inside the rounding. The figure is worth computing rather than estimating because it is the number that turns a retention requirement into a procurement conversation, and it is usually the first time anybody has put the two together: the requirement was written as a period and the storage is what the period costs. The number also reframes whether every category of record needs that period, since a requirement applied to all record types at once is usually applied well beyond the classes it was written for, and one terabyte is not a large number in an estate that already stores a great deal. Each tempting wrong answer comes from one slip: 36,000 is the answer in gigabytes rather than terabytes, 3.6 drops a factor of ten, and 0.36 drops two.
questions.hint: Multiply the daily figure by the number of days, then convert gigabytes to terabytes.

questions.explanation: Ninety-six people interacted with the message and five in every six of them were recently trained, so one in six is the untrained group, and a sixth of 96 is 16. The second route gives the same figure: five sixths of 96 is 80, and 96 minus 80 is 16. The number is the point of the question rather than the arithmetic, because 96 is the figure a programme would normally report and 16 is the figure that bears on whether the training is working, and the difference between them is a change of population rather than a rounding difference. The aggregate of 96 moves with the size of the trained group, so a quarter in which the module is pushed hard produces a better number whether or not the untrained group changed at all, which is how a programme can report a falling click rate for a year while nothing has improved for the people it is aimed at. The common wrong answers are 96, which is the whole click count and is already in the report; 80, which is the trained group who clicked and who are the least interesting population here; and 24, which inverts the fraction by treating the untrained as five in six. The reporting change the number implies is to break the result out by training recency and to count against messages actually delivered rather than sent.
questions.hint: Find the untrained share of the clickers, then apply that share to the click count.
